summary: Psalm 7 begins with a speaker taking refuge in Yahweh while pursued by enemies. The speaker denies wrongdoing, asks Yahweh to judge the peoples, describes God as a righteous judge, and pictures violence returning on the violent. The psalm ends with thanks and praise to Yahweh Most High.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows how a psalm of danger can move from plea to appeal for judgment to praise. Within Book I of Psalms, it belongs among David-associated prayers of distress and trust.

context.author: The heading associates the psalm with David, but such headings may mark authorship, association, dedication, or belonging; their exact historical force is debated.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also receiving Psalms as prayer and Scripture.
context.date: Psalms is an anthology formed over time; assigning one date to Psalm 7 from this chapter alone would overstate the evidence.
context.setting: The poem speaks from danger, accusation, and pursuit, and its heading names Cush, the Benjamite, but the chapter does not explain that situation further.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and prayer: a David-associated lament or plea that uses vivid images, direct address to Yahweh, and a final vow of praise.

outline.heading: Taking Refuge
outline.note: The speaker turns to Yahweh for rescue from pursuers pictured like a tearing lion.

outline.heading: An Oath of Innocence
outline.note: The speaker invites severe consequences if he has committed the wrong charged against him.

outline.heading: Calling for Judgment
outline.note: Yahweh is asked to rise, gather the peoples, judge the speaker, end wickedness, and establish the righteous.

outline.heading: God the Judge and Shield
outline.note: God is described as shield, savior of the upright, righteous judge, and one who readies judgment if a person does not repent.

outline.heading: Evil Recoils
outline.note: The wicked person's mischief and violence are pictured as returning on his own head.

outline.heading: Final Praise
outline.note: The speaker responds with thanks and song to Yahweh according to his righteousness.

keyVerses.text: A meditation by David, which he sang to Yahweh, concerning the words of Cush, the Benjamite. Yahweh, my God, I take refuge in you. Save me from all those who pursue me, and deliver me,
keyVerses.why: This opening gives the heading, the direct address to Yahweh, and the basic situation of refuge and pursuit.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh administers judgment to the peoples. Judge me, Yahweh, according to my righteousness, and to my integrity that is in me.
keyVerses.why: The speaker asks the judge of all peoples to examine his own case, which is central to the chapter's movement.

keyVerses.text: God is a righteous judge, yes, a God who has indignation every day.
keyVerses.why: This line states the chapter's view of divine judgment in compact form.

keyVerses.text: I will give thanks to Yahweh according to his righteousness, and will sing praise to the name of Yahweh Most High.
keyVerses.why: The psalm closes by turning the appeal for righteousness into thanksgiving and praise.

questions.question: Who is speaking in this psalm?
questions.answer: The heading says, “A meditation by David,” and says it was sung to Yahweh concerning Cush, the Benjamite. Davidic headings are ancient features of the Psalter, but readers differ on whether they always mean direct authorship or a broader association. The chapter itself presents a first-person speaker under pursuit and accusation.

questions.question: What is the danger in the opening?
questions.answer: The speaker asks Yahweh to save and deliver him from those who pursue him. Verse 2 pictures the threat as being torn apart like prey by a lion, with no one else able to deliver. The language is vivid poetry, so it shows the intensity of danger without letting us identify the exact event from this chapter alone.

questions.question: What does “Selah” mean here?
questions.answer: “Selah” appears at the end of verse 5. It is an uncertain musical or performance marker whose exact instruction is no longer known. It should be noticed as part of the transmitted psalm, but not treated as if its precise function were settled.

questions.question: Why does the speaker ask to be judged?
questions.answer: The speaker believes the accusation against him is false, so he asks Yahweh to judge him according to his righteousness and integrity. In verses 3-5 he even says that if he has done the wrong, the enemy may overtake him. This is not a general claim of sinless perfection; within the chapter it is a claim about the case being brought against him.

questions.question: Does the psalm ask for private revenge?
questions.answer: The speaker asks Yahweh to arise, judge, end wickedness, and establish the righteous. The chapter places judgment in God's hands rather than describing the speaker carrying out revenge himself. Still, the language is severe, and readers should distinguish the psalm's appeal to divine judgment from permission for personal retaliation.

questions.question: What does it mean that God searches “minds and hearts”?
questions.answer: Verse 9 says the righteous God searches minds and hearts. In this chapter, that supports the speaker's appeal that God can judge beyond appearances and accusations. The line does not explain the mechanics of divine knowledge; it states that inner life is within God's judgment.

questions.question: Who is the man in verses 12-13?
questions.answer: Verse 12 says, “If a man doesn’t repent,” and then describes sharpened sword and strung bow. The text gives a general picture of an unrepentant person facing prepared judgment. It does not name a specific person in these verses.

questions.question: What is the point of the hole and pit image?
questions.answer: Verses 14-16 picture evil as self-defeating: a person produces mischief and falsehood, digs a hole, and falls into the pit he made. The trouble and violence he causes return on his own head. The image makes moral reversal concrete without explaining every circumstance of how it happens.

questions.question: How does the ending fit the rest of the psalm?
questions.answer: The final verse does not say the danger has visibly ended. It says the speaker will give thanks and sing praise to Yahweh according to his righteousness. The ending ties praise to the same theme that ran through the appeal: Yahweh's righteousness as judge.

glossary.def: The word used in the heading for this psalm; the chapter presents it as something David sang to Yahweh.
A place or condition of safety; in verse 1 the speaker says he takes refuge in Yahweh.
Wrongdoing or guilt; in verse 3 the speaker denies that iniquity is in his hands.
Wholeness or uprightness in the matter being judged; in verse 8 the speaker asks Yahweh to judge according to the integrity in him.
Anger or opposition toward wrong; verse 11 says God has indignation every day.
A hole or trap; verse 15 uses it as an image of a violent person's plan turning back on himself.
